short_definition: An AI hallucination is when an AI model, such as a chatbot, produces information that sounds confident and plausible but is false, made up or unsupported by its sources.
explanation: Large language models generate text by predicting likely next words based on patterns in their training data. They are not looking facts up in a verified database by default, so they can produce fake statistics, non-existent citations, wrong dates or invented product features in fluent, convincing language.

It matters because people increasingly use AI assistants for research, money questions and business tasks. A hallucinated tax rule, interest figure or legal requirement can lead to costly decisions if it isn't checked against an authoritative source.

Tools that let the AI search the web or cite documents can reduce hallucinations but don't eliminate them. The practical trade-off is speed versus reliability: use AI to draft and explore, then verify important facts with official sources, the original documents or a qualified professional.
example: Illustrative example: You ask a chatbot for three studies on side-hustle income, and it lists three titles with authors and years. When you search for them, only one exists — the other two were hallucinated. Checking each citation took five minutes and avoided quoting fake research.
common_mistake: Trusting an answer because it is detailed and confidently worded, rather than verifying key facts, numbers and citations independently.
title: AI Hallucination
